blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Write up to 400 words that use the space well, in the vocabulary, style and structure the brief demands; adapt style across forms and audiences.

blocks.heading: Planning the 400
blocks.text: Planning up to 400 words means sharing them: an opening of about fifty words that establishes the form and the voice; two or three developed sections of about a hundred each, carrying the piece’s content with its ideas developed; and a close of about fifty that lands the purpose. The words are a budget, not a ceiling to bump against — and the budget exists because the table rewards development, which needs room.

blocks.heading: The opening’s job
blocks.text: The opening of a 400-word piece must establish the form and the voice at once, so the reader knows what they are reading and who is speaking before the first section arrives: a speech greets its hall, an email finds its reader, a report states its subject and its purpose. In a piece this short the opening is a fifth of the whole, and a slow opening is a fifth wasted — the strongest openings are already doing the piece’s work.

blocks.heading: Why length is development
blocks.text: A very short answer loses the development marks because development is part of achieving the task: the table rewards ideas developed — claimed, reasoned, exemplified, carried — and writing far less than the space allows leaves them named. A piece of 180 words for a 400-word task has usually produced a list where the table wanted a carrying, and its mark reads as the task only partly achieved, whatever the sentences are like.

blocks.heading: Worked example: audience changing the words
blocks.text: The same content for two audiences. For classmates: "Look, the trip is happening — we just need two more people to make the bus pay for itself, so this is me asking you before I have to ask a teacher." For the school board: "The Geography field trip requires two additional participants to reach the minimum number for coach hire; I write to request approval to open places to the neighbouring class." The facts are one set; the vocabulary, the contractions, the pronouns and the structures are two — because the audience changed, and the change is visible in every choice.

blocks.heading: Register is decided by the pair
blocks.text: Formal and informal register are decided by the audience and purpose, not in general: a formal register suits an official reader and an official purpose, and an informal one suits a friend and a friendly purpose, and each mismatches the other’s task as badly as the reverse. The test of register is not "which is better?" but "which reader, and for what?" — a formal blog misplaces itself as completely as a casual report to the board, and the analysis names the pair that decides it. Learn to hear the question in the brief itself: ‘to the parents’ says one register, ‘to the board’ says another, and the brief has opinions about it from its first word.

blocks.heading: In the exam
blocks.text: The shorter writing task is Paper 2 Question 1(a): a response of no more than 400 words to a prompt, choosing vocabulary, style and structure to fit a specific form, purpose and audience, and it carries fifteen marks — expression and range, accuracy, organisation and development, task achievement, and the audience’s engagement, all five strands in one table. The part (b) commentary that follows is written about this piece, so its choices matter twice: write the piece as a text worth analysing, with choices you can name. The next section teaches the commentary that will analyse it; this one teaches the piece that gives the commentary something to say.
